committee_name.text: Peripheral and Central Nervous System (PCNS) Drugs Advisory Committee

quote.quote: A meeting of the Peripheral and Central Nervous System Drugs Advisory Committee was held via an online teleconference on November 6, 2020.
A meeting of the Peripheral and Central Nervous System Drugs Advisory Committee was held via an online teleconference on November 6, 2020.

recommendation.text: The committee voted overwhelmingly against effectiveness. On whether Study 302 (viewed independently of Study 301) provides strong evidence of effectiveness, the vote was Yes: 1, No: 8, Uncertain: 2; on whether it is reasonable to consider Study 302 as primary evidence of effectiveness, the vote was Yes: 0, No: 10, Uncertain: 1. The panel largely endorsed the statistical review's skeptical conclusions and did not endorse approval.

linkages.concern: The advisory committee concluded it was unable to evaluate the effectiveness evidence from the positive Study 302 independently of the negative Study 301, and members doubted the clinical meaningfulness of Study 302's results; the panel largely endorsed the statistical review's conclusion that effectiveness on clinical endpoints was not established.
linkages.change: FDA did not grant traditional approval based on clinical benefit; instead it granted accelerated approval based on the surrogate endpoint of reduction in brain amyloid beta plaque, which it determined was reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit.

concern_quote.quote: the committee members concluded that they were unable to evaluate the evidence of effectiveness provided by Study 302 independently of the results of Study 301. In addition, panel members expressed concern about the clinical meaningfulness of the results of Study 302.

change_quote.quote: the reduction in amyloid identified in aducanumab clinical studies is reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit in AD, and supports the accelerated approval of aducanumab.

linkages.concern: The committee agreed there was evidence of an effect on amyloid plaques but was skeptical that this amyloid effect translated into changes on clinical endpoints, reflecting residual uncertainty about whether the surrogate predicts clinical benefit.
linkages.change: A postmarketing requirement (PMR) was issued requiring a randomized controlled confirmatory trial to verify the clinical benefit of aducanumab in Alzheimer's disease.

concern_quote.quote: The committee mostly agreed that there was evidence showing an effect of aducanumab on amyloid plaques but were skeptical that this effect was related with changes on clinical endpoints.

change_quote.quote: In order to verify the clinical benefit of aducanumab, conduct a randomized, controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of aducanumab compared to an appropriate control for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.

summary: The Peripheral and Central Nervous System Drugs Advisory Committee met November 6, 2020, and voted overwhelmingly against the effectiveness case (Yes:1/No:8/Uncertain:2 on whether Study 302 gives strong evidence; Yes:0/No:10/Uncertain:1 on considering Study 302 as primary evidence), largely endorsing the statistical review's skepticism. FDA nonetheless approved Aduhelm, but shifted from traditional approval on clinical benefit to accelerated approval based on the amyloid-plaque-reduction surrogate, coupling that decision to a required post-marketing confirmatory trial (PMR) to verify clinical benefit. The review documents describe the AC concern and these regulatory changes but attribute the accelerated-approval pivot to the residual uncertainty from the negative Study 301 rather than explicitly to the committee vote, so the linkages are marked inferred.
